{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=theoretical+frameworks+machine+agency+accountability+autonomous+systems&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Authorship responsibilities of scientists who use AI research agents.\", \"abstract\": \"The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) tools capable of performing research independently, which we call AI research agents (AIRAs) is likely to significantly impact how science is planned, performed, reviewed, evaluated, and communicated. However, the expected gains in efficiency and productivity from the deployment of AIRAs should not undermine science's epistemic and ethical values, such as accountability, transparency, reproducibility, and rigor. In this paper, we revisit the AI authorship debate in light of the reported capabilities of AIRAs and argue that these tools do not qualify for authorship because they cannot be held morally responsible for their contributions. We also reject the use of the term \\\"scientist\\\" to refer to these tools and argue that human scientists who use AIRAs have three key authorship responsibilities: (1) to carefully oversee and manage AIRAs; (2) to accurately and appropriately disclose AIRAs' contribution to research; and (3) to be accountable for research involving AIRAs by addressing questions and concerns raised by the scientific community and the public. Finally, we consider some related researcher responsibilities that are topics for future research, including the obligation to monitor, audit, and evaluate the performance of AIRAs and the obligation to address the social, economic, legal, and environmental implications of using AIRAs.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fgene.2026.1954843\", \"pmid\": \"42908681\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13683075\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fgene.2026.1954843\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13683075\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\",…

In the event of them violating the law – violations that are not intended by the person deploying them – it is not clear who is legally responsible, thereby creating an accountability gap.  Accountability is important in international law because where there is an accountability gap; the victims’ right to a legal remedy is adversely affected.  There are four forms of accountability that I am going to discuss in this paper: individual, command, corporate and state responsibility.  Under individual and corporate responsibility, there is civil and criminal liability.\\n\\nIn summary, the arguments I make in this paper are: the above mentioned forms of accountability are complementary to each other; they are not alternatives to the exclusion of the other. weighted initial conditions
Yoel Drori ∗
Abstract
We determine the exact worst-case function-value suboptimality after N first-order oracle calls on
L-smooth, µ-strongly convex functions under a nonnegative weighted combination of the initial squared
distance, function-value suboptimality, and squared gradient norm. Excluding the case where no strict
improvement in function-value suboptimality can be guaranteed, the exact deterministic minimax risk in
dimensiond≥ 2N +1 is characterized by the unique solution of a single scalar equation involving anN-step
recurrence. The proof constructs an explicit hard instance for the lower bound and a constant-memory
first-order method, ITEM-wf (previously called ITEM-w), whose worst-case performance matches this
lower bound. On the standard initial conditions, the result recovers the exact convex bound attained
by the Optimized Gradient Method of Kim and Fessler, and establishes the minimax optimality of the
recently introduced ITEM-f method of Kim, Ryu, and Das Gupta for the initial function-value condition.
Keywords:first-order methods; oracle complexity; smooth convex optimization; weighted initial conditions;
exact minimax risk; zero-chains
Mathematics Subject Classification:68Q25; 90C25; 90C30
1 Introduction
Under the oracle-complexity framework of Nemirovski and Yudin, optimization problems are studied in
terms of the information that must be obtained from an oracle to guarantee a prescribed accuracy [ 14]. For
quadratic minimization, Krylov-information arguments yield exact finite-horizon minimax bounds, attained
by the conjugate gradient (CG) method [ 12, 13]. For the broader smooth convex and smooth strongly
convex classes, classical oracle-complexity results establish the accelerated rates up to constant factors [ 1, 8].
Determining the exact finite-horizon complexity in these classes likewise requires both sides of the problem: a
first-order method with a sharp worst-case guarantee and a matching hard instance showing that no method
can improve it.
